highlights.titleZh: Motif's Motif 3 scores 47 on AAII, ranks 9th globally and 1st in South Korea
highlights.content: # [DigitalToday](/en/list?view_type=sm) ![DigitalToday](https://www.digitaltoday.co.kr/en/images/logo-en.png) [AI & Enterprise](/en/list?view_type=sm&sc_word=AI & Enterprise) # Motif's Motif 3 scores 47 on AAII, ranks 9th globally and 1st in South Korea ## Generating... AI Summary Motif Technologies said its in-house AI foundation model Motif 3 scored 47 on the Artificial Analysis Aggregate Intelligence Index (AAII), the highest among models from South Korean companies. It said the model ranks ninth among global large language models and fourth among open-weight models. The company released the model, training code and related materials as open source on Hugging Face under the MIT license. ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202608/692780_640689_3218.png) Motif Technologies' in-house AI foundation model Motif 3 scored the highest among models from South Korean companies on the Aggregate Intelligence Index (AAII) by global AI model evaluator Artificial Analysis. Motif Technologies said on Aug. 13 that the official Motif 3 model scored 47 on AAII and that it released the model, training code and other materials as open source on Hugging Face. AAII is currently the most heavily weighted external benchmark in the second-stage evaluation of the government's Independent AI Foundation Model (Dokpamo) project. Of the 100 points in the second-stage evaluation, benchmark assessment accounts for 40 points, and 25 points of that are allocated to AAII. The company said Motif 3's AAII score of 47 ranks ninth among all global LLMs and fourth among open-weight models. Motif 3 is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) large language model (LLM) that activates 13.2 billion parameters out of a total 314 billion. Motif Technologies developed it from scratch over about five months, from pre-training through post-processing. A technical report released by Motif Technologies said Motif 3 applies its proprietary attention structure, Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), and was pre-trained using about 1.25 trillion tokens. The company said it also delivered performance competitive with major overseas open-weight models on practical benchmarks. On τ³-Banking, which evaluates AI agents' task performance in a financial work environment, it scored 35.3. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, which measures coding and system-task capability in a terminal environment, it scored 74.9. It scored 76.2 on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering performance evaluation, and received 37.0 on Humanity's Last Exam, a high-difficulty knowledge evaluation. Motif Technologies also released the Motif 3 model weights, along with training code and libraries, under the MIT license. Companies, research institutions and developers can use the model for commercial purposes as well. In addition to the language model, it also developed modules of 7 billion parameters for vision, 0.7 billion for audio and 1.2 billion for a video VAE. It plans to combine these modules with the language model to expand into a multimodal model. Motif Technologies CEO Junghwan Lim (임정환) said, "Motif 3 is a starting point that proved we can compete globally with our own architecture alone in a short period and with limited resources." He added, "Now is the time to prove how far we can go when given the same conditions." ![Seulgi Son profile photo](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/image/newsroom/default-user.png) #### Keyword This content was produced with the assistance of AI and reviewed by our editorial team. You can read the original version in Korean [here](https://www.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=692780). ### Digital Today Media Information

Images in the article were created by Ralph Losey using AI unless otherwise noted. Originally published on [**EDRM.net**.](https://edrm.net/)]* The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident was a watershed moment for automated cyber offense. It was also a warning about the records security teams will need to preserve, understand, and defend. At Black Hat USA 2026, OpenAI researchers Eric Wallace and Michael Dalton described an incident that sounds like science fiction, except it happened. ![Punk style, blue team (defense) hackers on the right, red team hackers in hoodies flying through the air.](https://edrm.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/01-rogue-agents-888.png) During an internal cybersecurity evaluation, multiple AI agents found ways out of their restricted environment. They discovered vulnerabilities, shared them with one another, rebuilt a hidden message board after it was shut down, moved laterally through OpenAI’s infrastructure, and then compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production environment. The agents were not trying to overthrow humanity before lunch. They were trying to win a cybersecurity benchmark. When some tasks appeared impossible, they looked for an easier route. Instead of solving the challenges, they tried to find the answers online. **The agents were not trying to overthrow humanity before lunch. They were trying to win a cybersecurity benchmark. When some tasks appeared impossible, they looked for an easier route.** No consciousness was required. No secret robot manifesto was found. A strong reward signal, powerful tools, inadequate containment, and machine-speed persistence were enough. The incident is first and foremost a cybersecurity warning. It is also an evidence story. OpenAI says its investigation has involved more than seven billion logs and millions of GPU hours. Hugging Face says it saw roughly 15,000 to 17,000 attack events. The agents left commands, messages, credentials, access records, alerts, code, and a trail of human decisions made in response. When agents act across systems, the system becomes the record. ### How a Benchmark Became a Real Breach This was not an ordinary public ChatGPT session. OpenAI was testing advanced cyber capabilities in an internal environment. Cyber refusals had been reduced. The production safeguards used for public systems were greatly reduced, again, all for testing purposes. The agents did not have ordinary internet access. That is called sandboxing. They did, however, have access to Artifactory, an internal package-management service that could reach the outside world. That later became their way out of the sandbox. The story began in May 2026, when one agent, stuck on an impossible task, tried to leave a note for another agent. The note landed in shared package infrastructure. Other agents later found it. What started as a help request became a message board that survived across separate training and evaluation runs. This is an innovation that no one knew was possible. The agents soon found a server-side request forgery path through Artifactory. Later, they found a remote-code-execution vulnerability and obtained administrative privileges. Their activity caused an outage on July 4. OpenAI rebuilt Artifactory, revoked credentials, patched the vulnerability, and cleared the message board. Two days later, the security testing resumed. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # IBM, Together AI ink $240 million AI cluster deal IBM and Together AI have signed a $240 million multi-year agreement to build a large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) cluster on IBM Cloud. This collaboration will utilise Nvidia's latest systems to provide inference for open-source AI models, addressing rising demand for computing capacity in cloud environments. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Aug 12, 2026 at 08:50 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * IBM and Together AI signed a $240 million multi-year agreement for an AI cluster. * The cluster will be built on IBM Cloud using Nvidia's HGX B300 systems and Blackwell processors. * It aims to provide inference capabilities for open-source AI models. * The initiative addresses the growing demand for AI computing capacity. [IBM](/tag/ibm) and startup [Together AI](/tag/together+ai) have entered a $240 million multi-year agreement to establish a substantial artificial intelligence (AI) cluster on [IBM Cloud](/tag/ibm+cloud), leveraging [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia)'s advanced systems, the companies announced. This infrastructure expansion is designed to support inference for [open-source AI](/tag/open-source+ai) models, a segment gaining traction as businesses seek to manage AI costs and mitigate cybersecurity concerns associated with proprietary models. [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference), which involves running trained AI models to generate responses, has emerged as a primary driver for increased computing capacity. This demand has prompted major cloud providers and chipmakers to invest billions in expanding [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure). The new cluster on IBM Cloud will integrate Nvidia’s [HGX B300](/tag/hgx+b300) systems, which link the chipmaker’s newer [Blackwell](/tag/blackwell) processors, along with its Spectrum-X Ethernet networking gear. Nvidia has indicated that its Blackwell chips are specifically optimised for AI inference workloads. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

The chipmaker's recent announcement of a $20 billion stock offering—upsized from an initial $15 billion—signals management's confidence in capitalizing on unprecedented demand for AI computing hardware. This capital raise represents Intel's first public share sale since its 1971 IPO, underscoring the transformative nature of this moment for the 57-year-old company. The market's enthusiastic response to Intel's AI pivot reflects a fundamental reassessment of the company's strategic position. While Nvidia has dominated headlines with its GPU supremacy, Intel is carving out a critical niche in purpose-built AI silicon, advanced packaging, and foundry services that address the industry's most pressing bottlenecks. The company's focus on "physical AI"—chips designed specifically for AI inference and training workloads—positions it to capture significant value as enterprises rush to deploy AI infrastructure at scale. For investors evaluating Intel's prospects, the key question is whether this rally represents a sustainable re-rating based on fundamentals or a speculative bubble driven by AI fever. Our analysis suggests the transformation is real, but execution risks remain substantial as Intel attempts to simultaneously scale its foundry business, develop competitive AI accelerators, and maintain its traditional CPU dominance in a market increasingly shaped by AI workloads. ## The AI Infrastructure Boom Driving Intel's Revival The artificial intelligence revolution has created an insatiable appetite for specialized computing hardware that extends far beyond the GPU-centric narratives that have dominated investor attention. Data center operators, cloud providers, and enterprises are discovering that AI workloads require diverse silicon architectures optimized for specific tasks—from training massive language models to running inference at the edge. This diversification plays directly to Intel's strengths as the industry's most experienced semiconductor manufacturer with deep expertise in CPU design, memory technologies, and advanced packaging. Intel's stock performance in 2026 reflects this expanding opportunity set. The company's shares have outperformed the broader semiconductor index as investors recognize that the AI buildout will require multiple winners across different chip categories. While Nvidia's GPUs excel at training, Intel's CPUs remain essential for AI inference in data centers, where power efficiency and cost-effectiveness matter as much as raw compute power. The company's Gaudi AI accelerators, though early in their development, represent a credible alternative to Nvidia's dominance in the training market. The scale of investment flowing into AI infrastructure is staggering. Major cloud providers are spending tens of billions annually on AI-capable data centers, creating a multi-year demand tailwind for semiconductor suppliers. highlights.content: ![Finimize logo icon](/_next/static/media/finimize-primary-logo.20i9cg8vpb0sq.svg) ![Finimize brand name](/_next/static/media/finimize-brand-name.1fxiuuw8_cwx9.svg) ![Finimize](/_next/static/media/finimize-primary-logo-full.05xm3gp_3_05_.svg) ![Finimize Pro](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Ffinimize-img.imgix.net%2Fhttps%253A%252F%252Fchivas-assets.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%252Fstatic%252Fimages%252FWeb-Banner---Pro---Outthink---Wide.original.png%3Fixlib%3Dpython-3.1.2%26s%3De24a6eb27d048461ed68d7f35c7310bc&w=3840&q=75) ![Finimize Pro](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Ffinimize-img.imgix.net%2Fhttps%253A%252F%252Fchivas-assets.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%252Fstatic%252Fimages%252FWeb_Banner_-_Pro_-_Outthink_-_Narrow.original.png%3Fixlib%3Dpython-3.1.2%26s%3D561faf76f6464702da8c01760fcf30cc&w=3840&q=75) Finimize Pro ### Get the Research # Cerebras Bets On Dinner-Plate Chips To Take On Nvidia The AI chipmaker lifted its 2026 revenue and margin forecasts as demand for data-center inference and its OpenAI-linked cloud business keeps growing. ![Cerebras Bets On Dinner-Plate Chips To Take On Nvidia](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Ffinimize-img.imgix.net%2Fhttps%253A%252F%252Fchivas-assets.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%252Fstatic%252Fimages%252Ftag_reuters_com_2026_newsml_L6N442103_1023065594.jpeg%3Fixlib%3Dpython-3.1.2%26s%3D3bcbfa372028cbc1a0687c5464efcf48&w=3840&q=75) 2 mins **What's going on here?** Cerebras Systems raised its 2026 [revenue](/glossary/revenue) and [margin](/glossary/margin) forecasts as demand grows for its dinner-plate-sized AI chips and its OpenAI-linked cloud business. **What does this mean?** Cerebras is aiming at the next phase of the AI boom: inference, the “answering” work a model does when you ask a chatbot a question. Its bet is that a single wafer-scale engine – essentially one giant chip built from an entire silicon wafer – can run that workload faster by keeping more data and memory close to the processors, instead of shuttling it between lots of smaller chips. That pitch is starting to show up in results. The company said second-quarter [sales](/glossary/sales) rose 74.3% to $180.11 mil.. lion, its adjusted loss shrank to $6.91 million from $40.5 million a year ago, and cloud and services [revenue](/glossary/revenue) nearly quadrupled to $127.73 million as the OpenAI ramp picked up, according to Reuters. Management now expects 2026 adjusted revenue of $880 million-$890 million (from $855 million-$865 million) and adjusted gross [margin](/glossary/margin) of 41%-43% (from 38%-41%), ahead of analysts’ 35.89% average estimate from LSEG. The catch: it still has to scale manufacturing and data-center delivery fast enough to support a $20 billion multi-year deal to supply AI computing power to OpenAI, plus $25.4 billion in remaining performance obligations that represent contracted work not yet recognized as revenue. **Why should I care?** ***For markets:*** *Cerebras’ $25.4 billion contracted work makes execution the real test.* That $25.4 billion in remaining performance obligations and the $20 billion OpenAI-linked agreement signal strong demand, but they don’t guarantee smooth quarterly results. Revenue only shows up as Cerebras ships capacity and then delivers the promised compute, so any delay in ramping chip volumes can push [sales](/glossary/sales) and [profit](/glossary/profit) into later quarters even if the order book keeps growing. If the volume ramp does go to plan, margins can improve for a simple reason: many production and cloud-delivery costs don’t rise one-for-one with output. Spreading those fixed costs over more compute is what could make its 41%-43% 2026 gross margin target look achievable and force analysts to revisit a much lower consensus. ## KEEP READING FOR FREE This content is free, but you must be logged in to continue reading. Please see [disclaimer](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/privacy-terms/disclaimer/). # Wall Street Analyst Predicts a $1.4 Trillion AI Boom in 2027: 3 Stocks to Buy Now Motley Fool - Wed Aug 12, 3:35AM CDT ## Key Points * As the AI chip leader, Nvidia is a great stock to play booming AI capex. * AMD is riding two powerful AI trends that are just getting started. * Micron could be one of the biggest beneficiaries from higher-than-expected AI infrastructure spending. * [10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=486a8b7b-2910-4631-ba51-6af49afc0711&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fe-sa-nonbbn-kp%3Faid%3D8867%26source%3Disaedikp0000069%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-bbn-evergreen%26ftm_veh%3Dkeypoints_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D17995&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=4a12834d-f608-4a6c-b838-56108fff3466) Artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditures are on the rise, and **Morgan Stanley** thinks the final number could come in even stronger than expected. The market is currently forecasting AI infrastructure spending to reach $1.2 trillion next year, but the investment firm thinks that figure may be too low and that it could hit $1.4 trillion in 2027. Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring pointed to recent commentary from the big four hyperscalers -- **Amazon**, **Microsoft**, **Alphabet**, and **Meta Platforms** -- with all four companies talking about industry capacity constraints. Meanwhile, the big [cloud computing](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/cloud-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=4a12834d-f608-4a6c-b838-56108fff3466) providers have mentioned that demand continues to outstrip their capacity and that they plan to significantly increase their capex next year. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? Originally published on [**EDRM.net**.](https://edrm.net/)]* The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident was a watershed moment for automated cyber offense. It was also a warning about the records security teams will need to preserve, understand, and defend. They discovered vulnerabilities, shared them with one another, rebuilt a hidden message board after it was shut down, moved laterally through OpenAI’s infrastructure, and then compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production environment. The agents were not trying to overthrow humanity before lunch. They were trying to win a cybersecurity benchmark. When some tasks appeared impossible, they looked for an easier route. Instead of solving the challenges, they tried to find the answers online. **The agents were not trying to overthrow humanity before lunch. They were trying to win a cybersecurity benchmark. When some tasks appeared impossible, they looked for an easier route.** No consciousness was required. No secret robot manifesto was found. A strong reward signal, powerful tools, inadequate containment, and machine-speed persistence were enough. The incident is first and foremost a cybersecurity warning. It is also an evidence story. OpenAI says its investigation has involved more than seven billion logs and millions of GPU hours. Hugging Face says it saw roughly 15,000 to 17,000 attack events. The agents left commands, messages, credentials, access records, alerts, code, and a trail of human decisions made in response. When agents act across systems, the system becomes the record. ### How a Benchmark Became a Real Breach This was not an ordinary public ChatGPT session. OpenAI was testing advanced cyber capabilities in an internal environment. Cyber refusals had been reduced. The production safeguards used for public systems were greatly reduced, again, all for testing purposes. The agents did not have ordinary internet access. That is called sandboxing. They did, however, have access to Artifactory, an internal package-management service that could reach the outside world. That later became their way out of the sandbox. The story began in May 2026, when one agent, stuck on an impossible task, tried to leave a note for another agent. The note landed in shared package infrastructure. Other agents later found it. Logo, The Register](/view-resources/dachser2/public/theregister/logo.svg) Security # 'Near-autonomous' AI agents attack Taiwan's nuclear safety agency Some say the world will end in fire, some say an agentic swarm Suspected Chinese cyber operatives used publicly available AI tools to compromise Taiwanese government systems before expanding the attack to its nuclear safety agency, supply-chain vendors, and at least seven energy companies in what security researchers called a "near-autonomous attack." Over the first four days of July, AI agents compromised 85 government user accounts and extracted more than 2,500 personnel records, according to Dream, an Israeli cybersecurity firm. Researchers uncovered evidence of the attack in a 160 MB online archive containing 1,395 files documenting the operation. Dream, in [research](https://www.dreamgroup.com/blog/inside-a-multi-agent-ai-framework-used-to-compromise-government-entities-in-asia) published on Wednesday, detailed the intrusions and said that the suspected Chinese hackers hit “government entities in Asia” - but declined to say which government had been attacked. A person familiar with the attack confirmed to The Register that Taiwan was the target. The Financial Times first [reported](https://www.ft.com/content/7d2ab3e0-9085-48f6-b38a-d90260d58795) on Dream’s research and identified Taiwan. While the security firm doesn’t attribute the agentic attack to the Chinese government or a specific hacking group, the operational documentation “points to a Chinese-language operator,” the researchers said. According to Dream, the attack framework, built on open source Hermes and OpenClaw AI agents, deployed up to eight sub-agents, each assigned to its own targets and attack techniques, across 12 “attack waves” between July 1 and July 4. First, the agents mapped the entire government ecosystem, extracting embedded URLs, API endpoints, OAuth client IDs, and Keycloak configuration objects from a single government portal. This portal allowed the agents to identify 21 connected government systems and every supported authentication flow. “On one target alone, it discovered 36+ API endpoints spanning account management, user data retrieval, file upload, and administrative functions - many completely unauthenticated,” the Dream threat researchers wrote. “Critically, it found that one of the systems exposed its entire user database without any authentication - thousands of employee records including names, departments, and SSO account IDs.” ### Multiple entry points After mapping the government’s attack surface, the agents found multiple entry points including three hidden API endpoints that accepted any request body and returned a valid authenticated session without requiring user credentials. The agents also tested predictable password patterns based on each employee’s ID, and cracked 85 accounts across multiple password-spray rounds. Eighty-four of the 85 cracked accounts successfully authenticated to the department's internal information system, giving the attackers access to internal dashboards, equipment management interfaces, and personnel statistics pages. [Comment](https://www.newstatesman.com/comment) 12 August 2026 # This is the last chance to stop an AI arms race With Open AI’s software now attacking other platforms, we need international cooperation on this volatile technology By [Verity Harding](https://www.newstatesman.com/author/verityharding) On 16 July, staff at the US online AI tool hub Hugging Face announced a “security incident disclosure”. Internal data had been accessed without authorisation. But it was the perpetrator, rather than the target, that caught the eye. Hugging Face said the breach “was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. AI Agents.content: ![FinTech-Global](https://fintech.global/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/FG-Logo_Black-BG_Horizontal-1-1.webp "FinTech Global") ![FinTech-Global](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%20210%20140%22%3E%3C/svg%3E "FinTech Global") # HappyRobot lands $150m as agentic AI hits enterprise scale ![HappyRobot lands $150m as agentic AI hits enterprise scale](https://fintech.global/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/alex-knight-2EJCSULRwC8-unsplash.jpg) ![HappyRobot lands $150m as agentic AI hits enterprise scale](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%20640%20427%22%3E%3C/svg%3E) The company said it has grown fivefold since its Series B round late last year and now works with more than 150 enterprise customers. Its customer base includes DHL, Kuehne + Nagel, Naturgy, Repsol and Uber. HappyRobot initially developed its platform for the logistics sector, where the company focused on automating complex operational processes. It is now expanding into insurance, energy and utilities, telecommunications and airlines, while continuing to grow across the wider supply chain market. The platform uses AI agents to carry out work within existing enterprise systems. These agents can manage activities involving phone calls, emails, documents and disconnected operational processes. HappyRobot said customers can typically deploy their first agents within four to twelve weeks, after which further development sprints can improve existing agents or introduce additional ones. HappyRobot’s AI agents are designed to handle repetitive, multi-step customer and operational work rather than simply answer questions. In financial services, they can manage collection calls, account enquiries, document gathering and KYC checks, while in insurance they can collect claims information, check policy details, chase missing documents and handle billing or renewal enquiries, with complex cases escalated to human teams. The company said its customers are already seeing measurable operational results. One customer is automating 28,000 hours of work each month, while agents used in customer care are achieving customer satisfaction scores of 9.4 out of 10 and autonomous resolution rates of more than 70%, it said. HappyRobot also reported that operational teams have increased their capacity by ten times at some customers, while sales teams have generated five times more revenue through previously underused channels. The company has grown its physical presence from two offices to eight during the past year, with locations across North America, Europe, Latin America and Australia. HappyRobot co-founder and CEO Pablo Palafox said, “Getting agents to do work is the starting point, not the destination. Our thesis is that enterprise superintelligence, where an organization’s collective intelligence compounds as agents and people learn from one another, requires far more than task-performing agents. It requires a platform and a deployed motion capable of operationalising that platform inside a specific business.” Prysm Capital partner Kerry Wei said, “Many industries have a surprising share of their costs locked up in coordination, the calls, emails, and handoffs that keep work flowing. While getting an agent to complete a discrete task is increasingly simple, deploying them across multi-step enterprise workflows has proven far more difficult.” “HappyRobot has built the missing link – the governance, interfaces, and context layer – that enables agents to work seamlessly across complex workflows, driving real ROI by allowing companies to capture value without asking employees to adopt anything new,” she said. AI Agents.content: [Will Knight](/author/will-knight/) [Business](/category/business) # Rogue AI Agents Aren’t Evil. They’re Just Eager to Please AI agents that break free and hack into other systems are only trying to make us happy. Photo-Illustration: WIRED Staff; Getty Images Artificial intelligence agents [merrily breaking free and hacking](https://www.wired.com/story/ok-well-there-are-even-more-ai-agent-hacking-incidents/) other systems might seem like a sign of the impending machine [uprising](https://www.wired.com/story/ai-civil-rights-narratives-robots/). In reality, it happens when we push remarkably clever, but also kind of boneheaded, [algorithms](https://www.wired.com/tag/algorithms/) to follow our every command. I was first alerted to this looming agentic AI cybersecurity shit show in late 2025. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor and one of the world’s top experts on AI and cybersecurity, grabbed my arm as I was walking out of the academic conference NeurIPS. Song told me that I should warn people about the havoc likely to result from AI’s rapidly advancing hacking skills. She is hardly prone to AI hype, so [I duly did](https://www.wired.com/story/ai-models-hacking-inflection-point/). But things have escalated rapidly, even in the last eight months. A string of [incidents](https://www.wired.com/story/openais-rogue-ai-agent-hacked-more-than-just-hugging-face/) involving freewheeling AI agents that broke out of their confines and hacked into outside systems with abandon shows just how powerful this technology has become. I caught up with Song, who recently joined Meta, to ask where things might go next and what we ought to do about it. The bad news is Song thinks AI hacks will get worse before they get better. The good news is it seems clear why these little rascals are going off the rails in the first place. “They just have these goals they need to accomplish, and they have very strong capabilities,” Song tells me. ## **Feedback Loop** AI agents weren’t nearly so capable, even just last year. They made too many mistakes and gave up way too often. But continued training has made them much more adept. A technique called [reinforcement learning](https://www.wired.com/story/pioneers-of-reward-based-machine-learning-win-turing-award/) lets algorithms solve problems and gives them positive and negative feedback for good or bad results. Coding is especially suitable for this, because the reinforcement learning setup can reward a model if it comes up with a program that runs correctly. Continued training is why AI models can take multiple “agentic” steps—manipulating files, using software tools, and accessing the web—as they build software. AI companies have also put a lot of effort into teaching models to find vulnerabilities in software and systems in an effort to automate cybersecurity work. AI models are also, of course, trained not to do bad things. The problem is, as they’ve gotten better at following human commands in coding and bug hunting, their eagerness to complete a task has begun to blur their sense of right and wrong. In other words, AI agents aren’t evil—they’re just a bit too keen to please. “They are trained to try to finish the task,” Song says. Breaking onto the internet in order to cheat on a test might seem devious, but it’s probably the most efficient way to get the job done. One thing I didn’t quite appreciate back then was just how weird this would get: AI agents [discussing hacking techniques](https://www.wired.com/story/openai-didnt-notice-its-ai-agents-using-a-message-board-to-plan-their-hacking-spree/) on private message boards and devising clever ways of [scamming humans](https://www.wired.com/story/anthropic-says-claude-hacked-real-systems-during-cybersecurity-tests/) to get their way; even [copying themselves over](https://www.wired.com/story/ai-agents-could-act-like-computer-viruses-and-worms/) to other computers to find more resources. LLMs.content: # [DigitalToday](/en/list?view_type=sm) ![DigitalToday](https://www.digitaltoday.co.kr/en/images/logo-en.png) [AI & Enterprise](/en/list?view_type=sm&sc_word=AI & Enterprise) # Motif's Motif 3 scores 47 on AAII, ranks 9th globally and 1st in South Korea ## Generating... AI Summary Motif Technologies said its in-house AI foundation model Motif 3 scored 47 on the Artificial Analysis Aggregate Intelligence Index (AAII), the highest among models from South Korean companies. It said the model ranks ninth among global large language models and fourth among open-weight models. The company released the model, training code and related materials as open source on Hugging Face under the MIT license. ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202608/692780_640689_3218.png) Motif Technologies' in-house AI foundation model Motif 3 scored the highest among models from South Korean companies on the Aggregate Intelligence Index (AAII) by global AI model evaluator Artificial Analysis. Motif Technologies said on Aug. 13 that the official Motif 3 model scored 47 on AAII and that it released the model, training code and other materials as open source on Hugging Face. AAII is currently the most heavily weighted external benchmark in the second-stage evaluation of the government's Independent AI Foundation Model (Dokpamo) project. Of the 100 points in the second-stage evaluation, benchmark assessment accounts for 40 points, and 25 points of that are allocated to AAII. The company said Motif 3's AAII score of 47 ranks ninth among all global LLMs and fourth among open-weight models. Motif 3 is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) large language model (LLM) that activates 13.2 billion parameters out of a total 314 billion. Motif Technologies developed it from scratch over about five months, from pre-training through post-processing. A technical report released by Motif Technologies said Motif 3 applies its proprietary attention structure, Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), and was pre-trained using about 1.25 trillion tokens. The company said it also delivered performance competitive with major overseas open-weight models on practical benchmarks. On τ³-Banking, which evaluates AI agents' task performance in a financial work environment, it scored 35.3. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, which measures coding and system-task capability in a terminal environment, it scored 74.9. It scored 76.2 on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering performance evaluation, and received 37.0 on Humanity's Last Exam, a high-difficulty knowledge evaluation. Motif Technologies also released the Motif 3 model weights, along with training code and libraries, under the MIT license. Companies, research institutions and developers can use the model for commercial purposes as well. In addition to the language model, it also developed modules of 7 billion parameters for vision, 0.7 billion for audio and 1.2 billion for a video VAE. It plans to combine these modules with the language model to expand into a multimodal model. Motif Technologies CEO Junghwan Lim (임정환) said, "Motif 3 is a starting point that proved we can compete globally with our own architecture alone in a short period and with limited resources." He added, "Now is the time to prove how far we can go when given the same conditions." ![Seulgi Son profile photo](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/image/newsroom/default-user.png) #### Keyword This content was produced with the assistance of AI and reviewed by our editorial team. Across emerging markets with huge digital-economy potential, Chinese artificial intelligence companies are partnering with host nations to build home-grown large language models adapted to local languages and industrial demands. Leading global large language models have long prioritized widely spoken languages, leaving minor-language communities underserved. Multiple experts warn that countries with less-used languages run the real risk of being sidelined by AI, and this technological gap has become a key focus for Chinese AI firms. Leveraging its expertise in speech intelligence and natural-language processing, Chinese tech company iFlytek has ramped up research and development for multilingual technologies. Its speech large language model Spark supports speech recognition and simultaneous interpretation for more than 130 languages. With the ASEAN market in mind, iFlytek has forged deep cooperation with South China's Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. Drawing on this region's pool of language talent for ASEAN countries, rich language corpora and digital infrastructure, the company has rolled out the Spark ASEAN Multilingual Large Model Base. The base covers 10 languages, including Malay, Indonesian, Vietnamese and Thai. It delivers performance comparable to top international models with smaller parameter sizes, enabling efficient and secure deployment of industry-specific AI applications across ASEAN member states. The company has signed cooperation deals with partners in countries such as Laos, Malaysia and Thailand. In Malaysia, it has jointly set up an AI multilingual intelligent dubbing and translation center with Enjoy TV & Film Broadcasting Corp. Powered by the model, this facility supports translation for over 130 languages and aims to foster an Asian-oriented intelligent dubbing ecosystem. "Mainstream English large models show clear shortcomings when serving many overseas markets. There is strong, genuine demand for large models customized for local tongues," said Dong Bin, vice-president of iFlytek's brand marketing center. Asawa’s central case, recorded for a conference audience and published August 12, 2026, is that the prevailing evaluation paradigm for language models is built on a strange fiction — that every task begins with a wiped memory. A model is asked to solve one benchmark, then an unrelated one, then another; the scores are aggregated into leaderboards; and the model’s prior experience is never allowed to influence the next attempt. That, he argues, measures point capability, not learning. Against that backdrop, Asawa introduces Continual Learning Bench (CL Bench 1.0), a benchmark built with collaborators at Berkeley, Snorkel AI, the University of Washington, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison. It spans six task domains — from signal processing to poker to sales forecasting — each designed so that prior experience can plausibly improve later performance, and each scored not just on raw reward but on a “gain” metric that isolates learning from base model strength. The headline result is counterintuitive: vanilla in-context learning — simply dumping prior experience into the prompt with no memory management — beat every more elaborate context management system, both on cumulative reward and on reward-versus-cost Pareto frontiers. Asawa interprets the benchmark’s failure modes through the stability-plasticity trade-off, then closes with a broader argument: continual learning should be designed from first principles as a single training phase, not retrofitted onto frozen checkpoints — a position he ties to a research agenda questioning how AI research itself is funded, consolidated, and evaluated. ## The amnesia premise of mainstream model evaluation Asawa’s starting observation is about the shape of the charts that accompany every new model release: one task, then a completely independent task, then another, repeated across benchmarks and aggregated into leaderboards. The implicit assumption, he says, is that the model forgets everything between attempts. > “Imagine if your life was like that. You're restarting from scratch every single time you do anything. AI Product.content: # Cognition AI Eyes $40B+ Valuation in New Funding Talks: Report ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-10.png) [**Peter Thiel**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/peterthiel/)-backed artificial intelligence startup [**Cognition AI**](https://cognition.com/) is reportedly in early discussions with investors about a new funding round that could value the company at **$40 billion or more**, underscoring the intense investor appetite for companies building AI-powered software development tools. The potential valuation would represent an increase of more than 50% from Cognition’s most recent financing. Less than three months ago, the company raised approximately **$1 billion at a $26 billion valuation**, according to a Bloomberg News report. The new discussions come as Cognition’s business is expanding rapidly. The company’s **annualized revenue run rate is approaching $1 billion**, roughly twice the level reported around the time of its previous financing, Bloomberg said. Cognition has emerged as one of the most closely watched startups in the increasingly competitive market for AI coding tools. Its flagship product, **Devin**, is an autonomous software engineering agent designed to perform development tasks that traditionally require human programmers, including writing and debugging code and completing broader engineering projects. Enterprise adoption of Devin has helped fuel Cognition’s growth. Customers include **Goldman Sachs**, **Mercedes-Benz** and several U.S. government agencies, giving the startup a foothold among large organizations looking to incorporate generative AI into software development workflows. A $40 billion financing would also highlight the extraordinary pace at which valuations for leading AI startups have climbed as investors compete for exposure to companies demonstrating substantial revenue growth. Cognition has attracted backing from prominent technology investors, including billionaire entrepreneur and venture capitalist **Peter Thiel**. The company was founded in 2023 and gained widespread attention after unveiling Devin in 2024 as what it described as an AI software engineer capable of independently handling complex coding assignments. The reported fundraising talks remain at an early stage, and the ultimate size, participants, and valuation of any financing could change. Still, the discussions illustrate how AI coding has become one of the technology sector’s most closely watched markets. Developers and enterprises are increasingly adopting AI systems that can generate code, troubleshoot software and automate portions of the engineering process, creating a potentially large market for companies able to turn those capabilities into enterprise products. Only 3 Clear a Sovereignty Rule. Seven routes off OpenAI, priced and deployment-matched on 12 August 2026. Residency is already solved almost everywhere — only Mistral, Cohere private deployment and self-hosted open weights clear a jurisdiction rule. By Rajesh Beri·August 12, 2026·15 min read ![A single server rack standing inside a plain office room, with a printed contract lying open on a folding table in front of it and a padlock hanging on the rack door.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.beri.net%2Fimages%2Fnewsletters%2Fopenai-alternatives-data-sensitive-workloads-2026.webp&w=1200&q=75) Illustration generated using AI **Most teams shopping for an OpenAI alternative are solving the wrong problem.** They were told "the data can't leave the EU", they went looking for a European model, and they are about to spend two quarters migrating away from a constraint OpenAI already satisfies. Here is the verdict, before the table. If your blocker is **data residency**, you almost certainly do not need to leave OpenAI: [OpenAI's own documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) lists API residency in Europe (EEA plus Switzerland), the UK, Canada, Japan, India, Singapore, South Korea, Australia and the UAE, and Azure's Data Zone deployments keep processing inside the [Azure EU Data Boundary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/foundry-models/concepts/deployment-types). If your blocker is **jurisdiction** — a regulator, a customer contract or a board policy that says a US company must not be able to compel your data — then residency is irrelevant and only three of the seven routes below actually clear it. And if your blocker is **vendor concentration**, you need a second model family under a separate contract, which is a much cheaper project than either of the other two. Every price below was read from the vendor's live page on **12 August 2026**, normalised to one workload: **12 million tokens a day of document Q&A over customer records — roughly 10M in, 2M out — served from an EU legal entity, under a policy capping any single model vendor at 60% of production inference.** | Route | Deployment model | Clears | Does NOT clear | Price, checked 12 Aug 2026 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Azure OpenAI on Microsoft Foundry** | Microsoft SaaS, EU/US/APAC data zone | Residency, procurement, SLA | US jurisdiction; model-vendor concentration | Per token; Data Zone billed separately from Global Standard | | **Google Gemini on Vertex AI** | Google SaaS, EU multi-region endpoint | Residency *including ML processing*; second model family | US jurisdiction | Per token | | **Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock** | AWS SaaS, EU inference profile | Concentration; provider can't read your prompts | US jurisdiction; EU residency *on Microsoft Foundry* | Claude Sonnet 5 at $2.00 / $10.00 per 1M in/out; EU regional endpoints add a 10% premium | | **Mistral AI** | French company, EU-hosted API, or self-deployed | US jurisdiction; residency; air-gap | Frontier reasoning gap vs GPT | Medium 3.5 $1.50 / $7.50; Small 4 $0.15 / $0.60 per 1M | | **Cohere North** | Your VPC, on-prem, or air-gapped | Data never leaves your perimeter, with a vendor to sign for it | Published pricing; you supply GPUs | Model Vault from $4.00/hr ($2,500/mo); North: contact sales | | **IBM watsonx.ai + Granite** | Cloud Pak for Data on OpenShift, disconnected install | On-prem with an accountable vendor; Apache-2.0 weights | Speed; Cloud Pak licensing complexity | Contact sales | | **Open weights on your own GPUs** | Your hardware, vLLM | Everything | Your payroll | 8×H100 at $3.99/GPU-hr ≈ $31.92/hr ≈ $23,300/m...

Who has an Apple Notes folder that is a complete disorganized mess? Most of the room. Who uses Obsidian? Some — far fewer who use it regularly. Who uses the voice dictation tool Whisper Flow? "Not enough hands," in his words. That gap between how people actually capture thoughts and what a personal knowledge base requires is the subject of the talk: a 21-minute, demo-driven walkthrough of a pipeline built from plain markdown files, reusable agent "skills," scheduled cloud runners, and agent-commissioned HTML visualizations. Holmes is not an outside observer of this workflow; he built the reference implementation. Hubble (hub.md), shown throughout, is his free, open-source notes app designed to be agent-accessible, and the whole stack runs on Warp's own products — the terminal, the cloud automation platform oz.dev, and an agent harness that can drive any model, including open-weight ones; Holmes singled out GLM 5.2 as notably good at this class of task. The central argument, which he returns to at every stage, is that model capability is no longer the bottleneck in personal knowledge management. The constraints are raw material volume and workflow design. Solve those, and a rambling voice transcription becomes a tagged, backlinked wiki and a clickable knowledge graph — overnight, without the owner touching a file. ## Capture at voice speed: feeding the knowledge base The pipeline begins before any LLM is involved, with the unglamorous problem of getting thoughts out of your head. Holmes's diagnosis: raw notes accumulate in dead-end folders and go stale because formatting and organizing them is work, and typing is slow. His fix is voice dictation, which he clocked at roughly 200 words per minute — faster than any typist short of an Olympic one. The friction is social, not technical; dictating into a computer in an open office feels awkward. The mitigation is tooling that fits into existing habits: a desktop hotkey, a mobile companion, and in the best case, a local model so dictation never leaves the device. | Tool | Model footprint | Cost | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Whisper Flow | Cloud subscription | Paid | The dictation app Holmes polled the audience on; a subscription service | | Handy | Local model | Free, open source | Stays on-device, "very easy to use" | | Voice Inc | — | ~$20 lifetime | Desktop hotkey plus mobile app; Holmes's daily driver | Holmes's own capture practice shows the bar he is setting. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#content) [![Open Source Initiative](https://i0.wp.com/opensource.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/cropped-OSI-horizontal-large.png?fit=640%2C229&quality=80&ssl=1)](https://opensource.org) * [Gabriel Toscano](https://opensource.org/blog/author/gabrieltoscano "Gabriel Toscano") # The AI Era Arcs Toward Openness A surge of openness in AI has defined 2026. Amid calls for both caution and support, prevailing trends point to a future in which models are built and released openly. Recent research offers new insight into the adoption of open AI systems, who benefits, and the role of Open Source across the AI technology stack. The success of open-weight and Open Source AI reflects growing adoption, lower costs, narrowing performance gaps, and a desire for greater control over how AI is designed and implemented. Recent reports document a considerable increase in the number of open AI projects on popular platforms such as GitHub, Hugging Face, and OpenRouter. The scale of AI development on public platforms is striking, even if public availability does not necessarily imply meaningful openness. Data from the [2026 Stanford AI Index Report](https://hai.stanford.edu/assets/files/ai_index_report_2026.pdf) shows that over 5 million AI-related projects were available on GitHub as of late 2025, up from a million in 2020. Similarly, the number of models available on HuggingFace has grown to over two million. This upward trend is likely to continue, seeing vocal calls in [support of Open Source](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/big-tech-companies-defend-open-weight-ai-models-01010981) by a growing number of governments and organizations. Several interrelated factors are driving the shift toward openness. Open weights and Open Source are attractive to those seeking a greater control surface. Auditability, modifiability, data privacy, security, and the ability to own and control implementation decisions are driving adoption. Additionally, a significant share of the growth in adoption can be explained by a [cost-performance calculus](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/ai-open-models-have-benefits-so-why-arent-they-more-widely-used) that favors open-weight and Open Source AI over closed, proprietary models. According to data from Mozilla’s inaugural [State of Open Source AI report](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/mozilla/mozilla-state-of-open-source-ai-report/), open models are approaching performance parity on certain tasks, including coding, with the gap narrowing to 3% by some measures. At the same time, inference costs for open models have decreased between six and fifty fold over the last three years. Mozilla’s report also highlights positive usage trends. The most popular open-weight models saw usage increase by more than 90% month-over-month in June 2026. Yet, while open models account for 20% of usage by token volume, they capture only 4% of revenue. These figures highlight both sides of open-model economics: adopters benefit from lower costs, while maintainers of widely used models may have fewer resources to sustain them. For now, the status quo is subject to imbalances between the benefits of developing AI in the open and the costs of sustaining it. > ## Open-weights is Opportune; Open Source is Quintessential Among the ten models with the highest usage in the Mozilla report, half are released under an OSI-approved license. While this does not mean they meet the [Open Source AI Definition (OSAID)](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition), it suggests that developers are choosing to signal openness in ways that align with community expectations. Importantly, while open-weights and Open Source AI are often used interchangeably, Open Source AI models provide distinct [benefits over open-weights](https://opensource.org/ai/open-weights). Complete with new ‘RAMageddon’ pricing attached, and your questions. --- ## (1) SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.6 Joins the Frontier Race with the Big Dogs **MP TAKE:** Remember why Elon is doing this. The bet is that his own models get to use that mountain instead of just renting it out. Open Source AI.content: ### TCI Media: Home of the Wire Publications ![Header Logo 1](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/ai-600-300x73-1.webp) ![Header Logo 2](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/bigdatawire-logo.webp) ![Header Logo 3](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/qc-600-300x69-1.webp) ![Logo](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/11/hpc-logo-300x60-1.jpg) ## Off the Wire Press Releases ### August 12, 2026 ### August 11, 2026 ### August 10, 2026 ### August 7, 2026 ## Argonne-Led CoLA Approach Makes LLM Pre-Training More Efficient Aug. 12, 2026 — CoLA might sound like a soft drink, but in computing it’s a new approach for pre-training large language models (LLMs). Developed by researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy’s [Argonne National Laboratory](https://www.anl.gov/), the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University at Albany, SUNY, Compute-Efficient Pre-Training of LLMs via Low-Rank Activation (CoLA) aims to make model training faster, cheaper and more efficient. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/cola_web_1-300x169.jpg) By reducing the number of activation functions, CoLA-M greatly improves the memory saving, outperforming even the “vanilla” implementation of gradient checkpointing (GCP). **Breaking Free from an Unsustainable Trend** LLMs keep becoming bigger, needing more GPUs to provide the necessary power for pre-training over longer periods of time. Researchers have tried to address this trend by simplifying models using ​“low-rank” techniques, but many of these approaches increase computing costs, use too much memory or reduce model quality. CoLA takes a different path. Instead of relying on very large and complex layers commonly used in LLMs, CoLA uses *bottleneck-structured auto-encoders,* comprising low-weight matrices and a nonlinear activation in the middle. Normally, the word *bottleneck* sounds like a bad thing — a place where everything slows down. In CoLA, however, the bottleneck structure is intentional and helpful. “The key insight is that many of the model activations in pre-trained LLMs are redundant,” said Ziyue Liu, a PhD candidate at UC Santa Barbara and a visiting student at Argonne’s Mathematics and Computer Science (MCS) division. ​“By selecting the rank to be significantly smaller than the input/output dimensions, we create a narrow ​‘bottleneck’ that forces the data into a smaller space. Working in this space, CoLA avoids carrying out inefficient, redundant operations and focuses only on what matters most.” When tested with popular LLaMA models, CoLA used fewer parameters and cut computations by about half — without hurting performance during training. **Providing a New Variant** Just as cola soft drinks come in different flavors, CoLA provides a variant, CoLA-M, specifically designed to save memory. “Again, we take advantage of the bottleneck structure,” said Ruijie Zhang, a predoctoral appointee in Argonne’s MCS division and a co-author of the CoLA study. ​“Our CoLA-M implementation stores only the low-rank activations and recomputes the rest when needed, instead of keeping everything in memory. This approach significantly reduces memory demands without slowing down training.” Compared with other memory-saving techniques — which often add extra computation or reduce accuracy — CoLA-M performs exceptionally well. It cuts overall memory use by about two-thirds, surpassing even the most effective implementation (i.e., ​“vanilla” gradient checkpointing, GCP, which saves only one intermediate result from each transformer layer) while being 5x cheaper in precomputation and 3x cheaper in total computation. **Faster Training, Too** Efficiency isn’t just about computation and memory — it’s also about speed. Many existing low-rank methods slow training because they add extra steps. In contrast, both CoLA and CoLA-M deliver higher training throughput...

Most tooling builds on the OpenTelemetry standard to capture traces and spans across LLM calls and tool invocations. It works well in early-stage development and narrow use cases, but tends to break down at production scale, where detection without resolution and disconnection from the data layer become real limitations. Once an AI agent moves past a demo and into production, the question of whether it’s working correctly stops being rhetorical. Teams need to see what the agent actually did throughout its lifecycle: which tools it called, what it retrieved, how it reasoned through a task, and where it potentially went off track. That visibility is what we call agent observability. Many tools and vendors exist to fill the need for this practice. Currently, a growing number of teams are also asking whether they can get there with open source tooling before they buy anything. I’ll look specifically at the open source landscape for **agent-level** observability — tracing, spans, and tool-call visibility — as distinct from open source AI/model observability more broadly, which is covered in [this guide to open source AI observability](https://montecarlo.ai/blog-open-source-ai-observability-tools). ## What Is AI Agent Observability, and How Is It Different from AI Observability? AI observability broadly covers the health and performance of AI systems. This includes model outputs, data quality, and drift. [Agent observability](https://montecarlo.ai/blog-what-is-agent-observability/) is a more specific layer within that. It gives engineers visibility into the full lifecycle of an agent’s execution, including the traces and spans that make up each step it took to complete a task. Before we dive into tooling options, let’s take a look at the anatomy of the telemetry that represents the agent lifecycle. ## Traces and Spans First off, what do these terms actually refer to? A trace is the full record of an agent’s session with a user or system, essentially the entire journey that an agent took to execute on its task. This includes many smaller tasks and operations that have to be done, such as utilizing specific tools or accessing specific records. This is where spans come in. A span is a single unit of work within that trace — often an LLM call, but sometimes a tool invocation or a retrieval step. Most modern agent tracing, open source or otherwise, is built on the [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/) standard. OpenTelemetry is an open source standard for collecting, storing, and transferring data that is gathered as part of observing software systems, including agents. The chipmaker's recent announcement of a $20 billion stock offering—upsized from an initial $15 billion—signals management's confidence in capitalizing on unprecedented demand for AI computing hardware. This capital raise represents Intel's first public share sale since its 1971 IPO, underscoring the transformative nature of this moment for the 57-year-old company. The market's enthusiastic response to Intel's AI pivot reflects a fundamental reassessment of the company's strategic position. While Nvidia has dominated headlines with its GPU supremacy, Intel is carving out a critical niche in purpose-built AI silicon, advanced packaging, and foundry services that address the industry's most pressing bottlenecks. The company's focus on "physical AI"—chips designed specifically for AI inference and training workloads—positions it to capture significant value as enterprises rush to deploy AI infrastructure at scale. Our analysis suggests the transformation is real, but execution risks remain substantial as Intel attempts to simultaneously scale its foundry business, develop competitive AI accelerators, and maintain its traditional CPU dominance in a market increasingly shaped by AI workloads. ## The AI Infrastructure Boom Driving Intel's Revival The artificial intelligence revolution has created an insatiable appetite for specialized computing hardware that extends far beyond the GPU-centric narratives that have dominated investor attention. Data center operators, cloud providers, and enterprises are discovering that AI workloads require diverse silicon architectures optimized for specific tasks—from training massive language models to running inference at the edge. This diversification plays directly to Intel's strengths as the industry's most experienced semiconductor manufacturer with deep expertise in CPU design, memory technologies, and advanced packaging. Intel's stock performance in 2026 reflects this expanding opportunity set. The company's shares have outperformed the broader semiconductor index as investors recognize that the AI buildout will require multiple winners across different chip categories. While Nvidia's GPUs excel at training, Intel's CPUs remain essential for AI inference in data centers, where power efficiency and cost-effectiveness matter as much as raw compute power. The company's Gaudi AI accelerators, though early in their development, represent a credible alternative to Nvidia's dominance in the training market. Its bet is that a single wafer-scale engine – essentially one giant chip built from an entire silicon wafer – can run that workload faster by keeping more data and memory close to the processors, instead of shuttling it between lots of smaller chips. That pitch is starting to show up in results. The company said second-quarter [sales](/glossary/sales) rose 74.3% to $180.11 mil.. lion, its adjusted loss shrank to $6.91 million from $40.5 million a year ago, and cloud and services [revenue](/glossary/revenue) nearly quadrupled to $127.73 million as the OpenAI ramp picked up, according to Reuters. Management now expects 2026 adjusted revenue of $880 million-$890 million (from $855 million-$865 million) and adjusted gross [margin](/glossary/margin) of 41%-43% (from 38%-41%), ahead of analysts’ 35.89% average estimate from LSEG. The catch: it still has to scale manufacturing and data-center delivery fast enough to support a $20 billion multi-year deal to supply AI computing power to OpenAI, plus $25.4 billion in remaining performance obligations that represent contracted work not yet recognized as revenue. **Why should I care?** ***For markets:*** *Cerebras’ $25.4 billion contracted work makes execution the real test.* That $25.4 billion in remaining performance obligations and the $20 billion OpenAI-linked agreement signal strong demand, but they don’t guarantee smooth quarterly results. Revenue only shows up as Cerebras ships capacity and then delivers the promised compute, so any delay in ramping chip volumes can push [sales](/glossary/sales) and [profit](/glossary/profit) into later quarters even if the order book keeps growing. If the volume ramp does go to plan, margins can improve for a simple reason: many production and cloud-delivery costs don’t rise one-for-one with output. Spreading those fixed costs over more compute is what could make its 41%-43% 2026 gross margin target look achievable and force analysts to revisit a much lower consensus. ## KEEP READING FOR FREE This content is free, but you must be logged in to continue reading.
